notes:
Identity assessment: supplied cache is a Springer primary Original Investigation web parse, not merely an abstract. Title, all five named authors (Kathryn B. Francis, Michaela Gummerum, Giorgio Ganis, Ian S. Howard, Sylvia Terbeck), journal, volume 236, pages 3477–3496, year 2019 and DOI 10.1007/s00213-019-05314-z match the neutral replication reference. Methods, results, discussion and article metadata are present. Embedded Table 1 contents are not included (only its caption); supplementary DOCX is named but not supplied. No PDF was supplied, so no rendering was possible. Original, replication n and reported_success are unassigned placeholders and were not extracted. Target unresolved: the generic description and study identifier identify the experiment but do not distinguish the morality question from the behavioural question or BAC predictor from condition comparisons. Candidate p values: GEE condition effect using morality question p = .470, interaction p = .566; using behavioural question p = .286, interaction p = .480. Separate judgment chi-square tests in Fig. 5 caption: morality p = .492; behavioural p = .333. Peak-BAC prediction of the two judgment outcomes is reported collectively as ps > .109; this is a bound, not an exact p, and is not assigned to a single requested test. Virtual action BAC p = .575 concerns a different outcome. The printed h = −1.15 with Wald X2[1] = 27.18, p < .001 (morality-based model) and h = −1.27 with Wald X2[1] = 24.90, p < .001 (behavioural-based model) are TASK contrasts (action versus judgment), not alcohol–judgment effects. No alcohol–judgment coefficient/effect magnitude is printed in the inspected Moral responses result paragraphs. These task effect sizes must not be paired with alcohol-condition or BAC p values.
